findings.title: Filestore instance references a CMEK with no IAM grant letting the Filestore service agent use it
findings.explanation: google_filestore_instance.main sets kms_key_name = var.kms_key_name, which the example wires to google_kms_crypto_key.filestore.id. Setting kms_key_name alone does not grant Filestore's service agent (service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-filestore.iam.gserviceaccount.com) permission to use that key — GCP requires a separate IAM binding granting it roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter. A full repo search (grep for kms_crypto_key_iam, cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter, service_identity, gcp-sa-filestore) across both the module and example/examplea turns up nothing. Deterministic policy HLD_GCP_164 only checks that kms_key_name is non-null and passes here, so it can't see this gap — it doesn't reason about companion IAM resources at all. Without the grant, `terraform apply` fails at instance creation with a permission-denied error; this is the kind of thing a sibling module in this same author's portfolio (terraform-gcp-bigtable-backups, google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.cloud_run_cmek) already handles correctly for a different GCP service, making its absence here an inconsistency rather than an unfamiliar pattern.
findings.remediation: Add a service identity for the Filestore API and grant it the key: create google_project_service_identity (google-beta, service = "file.googleapis.com") and a google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member granting its email roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on google_kms_crypto_key.filestore.id. Add google-beta to example/examplea/terraform.tf's required_providers per this repo's own convention (beta providers belong in the implementation, not the module).

findings.title: Module defaults to Filestore's unrestricted, root-not-squashed NFS export options
findings.explanation: var.nfs_export_options defaults to null (variables.tf:173), and the dynamic "nfs_export_options" block in google_filestore_instance.main.tf:18-27 iterates local.nfs_export_options = coalesce(var.nfs_export_options, []) — at the module's own default, this produces zero nfs_export_options blocks. When the block is entirely absent, Filestore applies its own default: access_mode READ_WRITE, squash_mode NO_ROOT_SQUASH, ip_ranges effectively unrestricted to any client that can route to the share — i.e. every reachable client gets read-write access with root privileges preserved. I drafted and fixture-tested a deterministic policy for this exact gap (any_in over file_shares requiring nfs_export_options not_null) and confirmed it correctly fails a plain HCL block with no nfs_export_options — but run with --deep against this actual module, it PASSES google_filestore_instance.main, because the engine sees the dynamic "nfs_export_options" block declaration as syntactic presence without resolving that its for_each (local.nfs_export_options) evaluates to an empty list at the default variable value. This is a live instance of the 'dynamic block' blind spot: even the new rule can't catch this specific case, so it genuinely needs this kind of whole-config reasoning. The example's firewall rule (source_ranges = ["10.0.0.0/8"]) narrows network-layer reachability, but nfs_export_options is a share-layer control independent of that — relying on the firewall alone is a defense-in-depth gap, not a redundant control.
findings.remediation: Either change the module's default for var.nfs_export_options from null to an explicit restrictive default (e.g. scoped to the calling network's CIDR with squash_mode = "ROOT_SQUASH"), or, if an open default is intentional for a general-purpose module, document in the variable description that callers should set this explicitly for any deployment reachable from more than a single trusted client range — the current description already explains the default's effect but doesn't warn that root squash is also off.

suggested_policies.rationale: google_filestore_instance has no existing holden coverage for the CMEK-consumer IAM grant that GCP requires alongside kms_key_name (only HLD_GCP_164 checks that kms_key_name itself is set). This is a common, well-documented GCP gotcha across multiple CMEK-consuming services, each with its own service-agent email format; scoping this policy to Filestore's specific service agent keeps the check unambiguous. Validated structurally with `holden validate-policy` and fixture-tested: correctly fails an instance whose kms_key_name points at a key with no companion grant, passes one where a google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member on the same key grants cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter, and correctly skips (Unknown) instances with no CMEK at all. Known limitation: when kms_key_name is set via a module variable rather than a direct literal/resource reference, the linked_via value join can't resolve through the indirection even with --deep, so it silently misses the gap in module-based configs like this repo's own filestore module — worth noting for whoever reviews this, since it means the policy alone would not have caught HOLDEN_AI_001.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_474
name: Filestore instances using CMEK must grant the Filestore service agent key access
principle: key-management
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  Setting kms_key_name on a google_filestore_instance does not by itself grant
  Filestore's service agent permission to use the key. GCP requires the
  Filestore service agent (service-<PROJECT_NUMBER>@gcp-sa-filestore.iam.gserviceaccount.com)
  to hold roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the referenced key, via
  a separate IAM binding that Terraform never creates automatically. Without
  it, instance creation fails at apply time with a permission-denied error,
  and under time pressure teams sometimes work around this with a broader,
  ad hoc grant instead of a scoped binding.
remediation: |
  Grant the Filestore service agent access to the key:

    resource "google_project_service_identity" "filestore" {
      provider = google-beta
      service  = "file.googleapis.com"
    }

    resource "google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member" "filestore" {
      crypto_key_id = google_kms_crypto_key.main.id
      role          = "roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter"
      member        = "serviceAccount:${google_project_service_identity.filestore.email}"
    }
resources:
  google_filestore_instance:
    filter:
      path: kms_key_name
      not_null: true
    any:
      - requires_companion:
          type: google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member
          linked_via:
            from: kms_key_name
            to: crypto_key_id
          where:
            path: role
            equals: roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter
      - requires_companion:
          type: google_kms_crypto_key_iam_binding
          linked_via:
            from: kms_key_name
            to: crypto_key_id
          where:
            path: role
            equals: roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter

suggested_policies.rationale: No existing holden policy checks file_shares.nfs_export_options on google_filestore_instance (coverage_by_type lists only HLD_GCP_164, which checks kms_key_name). Filestore's documented default when the block is omitted is unrestricted read-write access with root squash disabled, which is exactly the kind of implicit-permissive-default pattern rules should catch explicitly rather than leaving to convention. Validated with `holden validate-policy` and fixture-tested against a plain (non-dynamic) HCL block: correctly fails when nfs_export_options is absent, passes when present. Known limitation, observed directly against this repo: when the block is built via a Terraform `dynamic` construct whose for_each resolves to an empty list (as in this repo's own filestore module, see HOLDEN_AI_002), the engine sees syntactic presence of the dynamic block and passes it regardless of the resolved value — this policy would not have caught the module's own default.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_475
name: Filestore file shares should not rely on default (unrestricted) NFS export options
principle: network-security
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  When file_shares.nfs_export_options is omitted, Filestore applies its own
  default: access_mode READ_WRITE, squash_mode NO_ROOT_SQUASH, and ip_ranges
  effectively unrestricted to any client that can route to the share. This
  means every reachable client gets read-write access with root privileges
  preserved (no root squash), with no share-layer restriction beyond
  whatever network-layer controls (firewall rules, VPC boundaries) happen to
  be in place. Explicitly setting nfs_export_options with scoped ip_ranges
  and squash_mode is defense-in-depth independent of network configuration.
remediation: |
  Set nfs_export_options explicitly on the file share:

    resource "google_filestore_instance" "main" {
      file_shares {
        capacity_gb = 1024
        name        = "share1"

        nfs_export_options {
          ip_ranges   = ["10.0.0.0/24"]
          access_mode = "READ_WRITE"
          squash_mode = "ROOT_SQUASH"
        }
      }
    }
resources:
  google_filestore_instance:
    path: file_shares
    any_in:
      path: nfs_export_options
      not_null: true
